Skorokhod problem

Words: 116 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
Find a constrained path and a boundary regulator which together modify a given driving path. In the half-line case, write x=g+k≥0, require k(0)=0 and k nondecreasing, and require its increases to occur only where x=0. For multidimensional orthants the regulator acts through a specified reflection matrix. The Skorokhod reflection map on the half-line solves the one-dimensional continuous-path case explicitly.

Skorokhod reflection map on the half-line (Γ(g)(t)=g(t)+sups≤t​[−g(s)]+)

Words: 61
Skorokhod problem OurBigBook.com
For a continuous driving path with g(0)≥0, the running supremum supplies the minimal nondecreasing regulator keeping the path nonnegative. It increases only at a new negative running minimum, where the reflected path is zero. Any regulator satisfying the Skorokhod problem constraints must coincide with it. On a finite time interval, ∥Γ(g)−Γ(h)∥∞​≤2∥g−h∥∞​, so the map is continuous and transfers a functional central limit theorem to reflected workloads.

Self-similarity of a stochastic process (Z(a⋅)=daHZ)

Words: 67
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A process Z is self-similar with exponent H if Z(a⋅) and aHZ have the same finite-dimensional distributions for every a>0, or the same path law when the process is considered as a random path. Fractional Brownian motion has this property with its Hurst exponent. It converts dilation of time to deterministic scaling of amplitude: Z(N⋅)/N=dNH−1Z. Consequently a small-noise large deviation principle with inverse-variance speed produces the large-deviation speed N2(1−H) for those rescaled paths.

Random field

Words: 42
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A random field is a family of random variables indexed by points of a spatial domain, or more generally by a multi-dimensional parameter set. Its componentwise covariance function and spectral tensor describe second-order dependence. A Gaussian random field has jointly Gaussian finite-dimensional distributions; a general random field need not be Gaussian.

Locally bounded process

Words: 47
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A process is locally bounded if there are stopping times τn​↑∞ and finite deterministic constants Kn​ bounding it on the stopped intervals. A locally bounded predictable process is integrable against a semimartingale. Continuous adapted processes are locally bounded by stopping their magnitudes and time.

Branching process

Words: 193 Articles: 2
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A stochastic process in which individuals independently produce offspring according to specified distributions. It models growing populations and gives an approximation to sparse percolation clusters when collisions between branches can be neglected. On a lattice, loops and overlapping branches prevent this approximation from being an exact identity.

Multitype Poisson branching process (Bi​(Λ))

Words: 150 Articles: 1
Branching process OurBigBook.com
A particle of type i has independently a Poisson distribution of type-j offspring with mean λij​. Different particles reproduce independently. If pi(t)​ is the probability generation t is nonempty from one type-i ancestor, then p(0)=1 and p(t+1)=T(p(t)), where Ti​(x)=1−exp[−(Λx)i​]. This iteration decreases to the survival probability of a branching process, the greatest nonnegative fixed point of T. The expected type-count row vector in generation t is eiT​Λt.

Spectral survival criterion for multitype Poisson branching (∑i​pi​>0⟺ρ(Λ)>1)

Words: 87
Multitype Poisson branching process OurBigBook.com
This criterion holds even for reducible nonnegative matrices. If a fixed point p=0 exists, 1−e−z<z for z>0 gives (Λp)i​>pi​ on its support. Some α>1 therefore satisfies Λp≥αp, forcing the spectral radius above one by the Perron–Frobenius theorem. Conversely take v≥0, v=0, with Λv=ρv and ρ>1. For sufficiently small η>0, 1−e−ηρvi​≥ηvi​. Thus ηv is a subsolution; monotone iteration under T gives a positive fixed point below 1. Strictness of 1−e−z<z excludes survival at the critical value for this Poisson offspring law.

Unnormalized time autocorrelation (C(t,τ)=⟨X(t)X(t+τ)⟩)

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
The raw same-observable time correlation C(t,τ)=⟨X(t)X(t+τ)⟩. For a stationary process, it equals ⟨X⟩2+Cov(X(t),X(t+τ)). Its connected part is the autocovariance; unlike the normalized statistical autocorrelation, no division by the variance is imposed. The distinction matters for fluctuations around a nonzero equilibrium point.

Intrawell phase autocorrelation (C(τ)≃α2+(Teff​/κ)e−κ∣τ∣)

Words: 60
Unnormalized time autocorrelation OurBigBook.com
Near the stable Adler phase equation point α=arcsin(ω/ϵ), linearized noise obeys an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with relaxation rate κ=ϵ2−ω2​. Its harmonic-model raw correlation is α2+(Teff​/κ)e−κ∣τ∣. Nonlinear drift also shifts the local mean at order Tmeff​. This describes times after relaxation but before appreciable phase slips; it is not a stationary infinite-time correlation of the unwrapped phase at fixed nonzero noise.

Sample path (t↦Xt​(ω))

Words: 55
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
For a stochastic process Xt​ and a fixed sample outcome ω, its sample path is the function t↦Xt​(ω). Statements about continuous, càdlàg or Hölder continuous function sample paths concern these functions simultaneously in time; they differ from assertions made only at each fixed deterministic time. A probability-one path property can be checked using countable dense times when the appropriate continuity is available.

Bounded increments (∣Xn+1​−Xn​∣≤C(n≥0))

Words: 238 Articles: 2
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A discrete-time stochastic process has bounded increments if a single deterministic C<∞ satisfies ∣Xn+1​−Xn​∣≤C almost surely for every n. The constant is uniform in time and sample outcome; bounding each increment by a different constant does not suffice. This property applies to differences, so it does not require the process itself to stay bounded.

Bounded-increment martingale convergence-or-oscillation dichotomy (Xn​→X∞​∈RorliminfXn​=−∞, limsupXn​=+∞)

Words: 186 Articles: 1
Bounded increments OurBigBook.com
A discrete-time martingale with a common deterministic bound on all increments either converges finitely or has liminfXn​=−∞ and limsupXn​=+∞, almost surely. Stopping on first crossing below −A gives a lower bound −A−M on the overshoot. Adding A+M+X0−​ produces a nonnegative martingale, so the martingale convergence theorem forces finite convergence on the event of never crossing. Apply the same argument to −X.

Oscillation of a bounded centered iid random walk (liminfSn​=−∞,limsupSn​=+∞)

Words: 126
Bounded-increment martingale convergence-or-oscillation dichotomy OurBigBook.com
Let Sn​=∑j=1n​Xj​, where the increments are nonconstant independent and identically distributed random variables with zero expected value and ∣Xj​∣≤c. Then the random walk oscillates between arbitrarily large positive and negative levels almost surely. For Ta​=inf{n:Sn​≥a}, the stopped martingale a+c−Sn∧Ta​​ is nonnegative. The martingale convergence theorem implies that Sn​ converges finitely on {Ta​=∞}. However, some δ>0 has P(∣X1​∣>δ)>0, and the Borel-Cantelli lemmas imply ∣Xn​∣>δ infinitely often. Hence finite convergence is impossible. Apply this to every positive integer a and to −Sn​.
The bounded increments also imply infinitely many visits to [−c/2,c/2]: a path cannot cross from above c/2 to below −c/2 without entering this interval. Identical distribution cannot simply be dropped. For independent symmetric signs εj​, the increments Xj​=c4−(j−1)εj​ satisfy ∣Sn​∣≥2c/3 for every n, even though they are nonzero, independent, symmetric and uniformly bounded.

Locally defined stochastic process ((X,T))

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A continuous locally defined process is a pair (X,T) specified on the stochastic interval [0,T), with a lifetime stopping time T approached by an announcing sequence for a stopping time Tn​. Each stopped process is an ordinary continuous adapted process. This is the convention used for continuous local differential equations; no value at T is required. Restricting a globally defined process gives examples, but finite lifetimes also allow approach to a domain boundary or explosion.

Local solution of a stochastic differential equation

Words: 64
Locally defined stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A local solution is a locally defined stochastic process taking values in a specified open domain U and satisfying the stochastic differential equation on every stopped interval before its lifetime. For dX=b(X)dt+σ(X)dB, the integral equation holds after each announcing stop, with the requisite local drift and noise integrability. A maximal local solution of a stochastic differential equation cannot be extended while remaining in U; a finite lifetime can be a boundary hit rather than divergence to infinity.

Stochastic interval ([0,T))

Words: 41
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
For a stopping time T, the stochastic interval [0,T) means the subset {(ω,t):0≤t<T(ω)} of sample-time space. Its endpoint varies with the sample. A locally defined stochastic process on it has no prescribed value at the endpoint. This notation is distinct from an ordinary deterministic interval.

Modification of a stochastic process

Words: 151 Articles: 2
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
Processes X,Y on the same probability space and index set are modifications of each other if P(Xt​=Yt​)=1 for each fixed index t. This differs from indistinguishability of stochastic processes, which requires equality at all indices on a single event of probability one. Equality at a countable dense set upgrades to indistinguishability when both processes have continuous paths.

Càdlàg modification

Words: 48
Modification of a stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A càdlàg modification of a stochastic process is a modification of a stochastic process whose paths are càdlàg on one event of probability one. Equality almost surely at every separately fixed time does not imply indistinguishability of stochastic processes when the original process lacks path regularity. A stochastic process starting at zero, with independent increments, stationary increments, and stochastic continuity, has a càdlàg modification and is a Lévy process under the intrinsic definition.

Continuous modification

Words: 48
Modification of a stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A continuous modification of a stochastic process is a modification of a stochastic process whose paths are continuous outside a single null event. For a process originally given only on a countable dense set, the analogous construction gives a continuous extension agreeing simultaneously at all original indices. The Kolmogorov continuity theorem and dyadic increment chaining are standard ways to obtain it.

Linear fluctuating interface (∂t​h=α∇2h+η)

Words: 118 Articles: 2
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A linear fluctuating interface smooths height gradients by diffusion and receives additive Gaussian white noise. With periodic or Neumann boundary conditions, its nonzero Fourier modes are independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes if the noise is diagonal in that basis. The unconstrained uniform height is a Brownian zero mode of a fluctuating interface.

Stationary spectrum of a linear fluctuating interface (⟨hq2​⟩=σ2/(2αq2))

Words: 35
Linear fluctuating interface OurBigBook.com
For a nonzero Fourier mode satisfying dhq​=−αq2hq​dt+σdWq​ with α>0, the explicit Ornstein-Uhlenbeck solution and Itô isometry give the stationary second moment σ2/(2αq2). The prefactor depends on the normalization of the mode noise, while the inverse-square dependence follows from diffusive relaxation.

Brownian zero mode of a fluctuating interface (dh0​=σdWt​)

Words: 47
Linear fluctuating interface OurBigBook.com
An unpinned uniform height driven by Gaussian white noise is Brownian motion. Its variance grows as σ2t and it has no stationary distribution on the real height axis for σ>0. Indeed, a stationary characteristic function would obey μ​(k)=μ​(k)e−σ2k2t/2, incompatible with continuity at zero. Quotienting out the uniform height can still leave stationary shape fluctuations.

Path probability

Words: 42
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A path probability is a probability measure, or a density relative to a specified reference measure, on histories of a stochastic process. A formal Onsager--Machlup path probability must be interpreted with its discretization and initial-state conditioning specified; conditioning on both endpoints produces a separately normalized bridge measure.

Langevin dynamics

Words: 25
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
Langevin dynamics describes a dynamical variable driven by deterministic forces and random noise. Underdamped Langevin dynamics retains inertia, whereas overdamped Langevin dynamics neglects it. At thermal equilibrium, the fluctuation-dissipation relation for a Langevin particle relates Gaussian white noise strength to drag and temperature.

Interacting particle system

Words: 2k Articles: 24
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
An interacting particle system is a stochastic process whose local states evolve through random transitions whose rates depend on nearby states.

Voter model (ξt​∈{0,1}V)

Words: 207 Articles: 3
Interacting particle system OurBigBook.com
At each site, a rate-one clock rings and the site copies the state of a randomly chosen neighbor. The model is a Markov process on Ising spin configurations, interpreted through its local update infinitesimal generator. All constant configurations are absorbing state. Tracing copying arrows backwards gives the voter-model duality with coalescing random walks.

Voter-model duality (ξt​(x)=ξ0​(Xtx​))

Words: 164 Articles: 2
Voter model OurBigBook.com
Independent Poisson process copying arrows construct the voter model. A backward ancestral line from a site follows a continuous-time random walk; lines that meet then coincide. Thus a finite collection of Ising spins at time t equals initial Ising spins at the positions of coalescing random walks. In particular Eη​ξt​(x)=∑z​pt​(x,z)η(z), and the probability of disagreement at two sites is bounded by the probability their ancestral walks have not yet coalesced.
Finite-seed local extinction in the voter model
Words: 47
Voter-model duality OurBigBook.com
If the initial one-spin set F is finite on the square lattice, voter-model duality gives P(ξt​(x)=1)=∑z∈F​pt​(x,z)→0. The transition probabilities tend to zero on this infinite lattice; their Fourier transform also proves the limit of a sequence by dominated convergence. A union bound on any finite set of observation sites then proves weak convergence of probability measures to the all-zero point mass in the product topology.
Invariant measures of the two-dimensional voter model (αδ0​+(1−α)δ1​)
Words: 59
Voter-model duality OurBigBook.com
In a nearest-neighbor voter model on the square lattice, any two ancestral coalescing random walks meet almost surely. For an invariant probability measure of a Markov process, the disagreement probability is constant in time but bounded by the vanishing probability of noncoalescence. Hence every pair of sites agrees almost surely. Countability concentrates the measure on the two constant configurations; both are absorbing state, so every mixture of their Dirac measures is invariant. Translation invariance need not be assumed.

Exclusion process (Lf(η)=∑x,y​p(x,y)η(x)(1−η(y))[f(ηxy)−f(η)])

Words: 395 Articles: 5
Interacting particle system OurBigBook.com
Particles on a countable lattice attempt jumps at the rates p(x,y), and an attempt into an occupied site is suppressed. Thus each site contains at most one particle and the number of particles is conserved when finite. Here ηxy interchanges the occupations at x and y. Bounded nearest-neighbour rates give a well-defined Markov process. A symmetric jump kernel gives the symmetric simple exclusion process; an unequal left-right kernel gives the asymmetric simple exclusion process.

Symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)

Words: 326 Articles: 4
Exclusion process OurBigBook.com
On Z, put independent rate-c Poisson processes on unoriented nearest-neighbour edges, and exchange their endpoint occupations at each mark. Its generator on cylinder functions is Lf(η)=c∑x​[f(ηx,x+1)−f(η)]. Equal occupations do not change the state, and a particle next to a vacancy jumps across at rate c. The stirring representation of symmetric exclusion constructs it for arbitrary initial configurations. The simple occupation-product product self-duality of symmetric exclusion requires symmetry and is not the ordinary duality of an asymmetric process.
Bernoulli invariant laws of finite symmetric exclusion (μρ​=⨂x∈V​Bernoulli(ρ))
Words: 66
Symmetric simple exclusion process OurBigBook.com
On a finite graph with symmetric edge-swap rates, the stirring representation of symmetric exclusion transports the occupations by a random permutation. An independent identically distributed Bernoulli distribution occupation field is invariant under every deterministic permutation, and hence under this random permutation when it is independent of the initial field. Therefore the displayed product measure is invariant, including densities zero and one. Equivalently, an edge swap preserves the number of particles and has the same reverse rate, giving detailed balance.
Stirring representation of symmetric exclusion
Words: 190 Articles: 2
Symmetric simple exclusion process OurBigBook.com
Give every site a distinct label and interchange labels at the edge marks defining the symmetric simple exclusion process. Each forward or backward label path makes only finitely many jumps in a bounded time interval, since its total rate is 2c. Occupations are transported along these paths. The backward ancestors of a finite set have the law of the finite-particle symmetric exclusion process, by time reversal of the Poisson marks. This proves the product self-duality of symmetric exclusion.
Product self-duality of symmetric exclusion (EηD(ηt​,A)=EAD(η,At​))
Words: 120 Articles: 1
Stirring representation of symmetric exclusion OurBigBook.com
For finite A⊂Z put D(η,A)=∏x∈A​η(x), with empty product one. Interchanging occupations gives D(ηxy,A)=D(η,Axy), where Axy interchanges membership of the two sites. The edge-swap generators therefore agree on D. The stirring representation of symmetric exclusion proves the displayed identity at all times by tracing the ancestors of A backwards. A general asymmetric jump kernel does not satisfy this product self-duality.
Exchangeable invariant laws of symmetric exclusion
Words: 61
Product self-duality of symmetric exclusion OurBigBook.com
If the probability of occupation at every site in a finite set depends only on its cardinality, the law is exchangeable. The product self-duality of symmetric exclusion and conservation of the finite dual particle count imply that all these occupation-product moments are unchanged by evolution. Inclusion-exclusion principle reconstructs every finite cylinder probability from them, proving invariance. This direct argument does not require a representation theorem for exchangeable laws.

Interacting particle system OurBigBook.com
In the contact process, infected vertices recover at rate μ, while each oriented nearest-neighbour edge transmits infection at rate λ. The empty configuration is absorbing.

The Brownian first-passage subordinator has a countable dense set of jump levels almost surely, and is continuous at every other level. Its paths are finite nondecreasing functions, so on a bounded level interval there can be only finitely many jumps larger than any fixed positive size; a countable union proves countability. For density, suppose its path were continuous throughout an open level interval. It is strictly increasing, since the original continuous Brownian path takes different values at different passage times. Its continuous inverse on that interval would parametrize a positive-length time interval on which the Brownian path increases monotonically. This contradicts nowhere monotonicity of Brownian motion. Thus every level interval contains a jump. In particular dense discontinuities do not mean that the path is nowhere continuous: it is continuous at every level outside a countable random set.

For a centered Gaussian random variable in a Banach space, its first Gaussian chaos is the closed linear subspace of L2 space generated by its continuous linear observations. Every element is a centered Gaussian random variable, and every finite collection has a multivariate normal distribution: approximate in L2 space and pass to the characteristic function. The first Gaussian chaos supplies the scalar coordinates of its Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian random variable in a Banach space.

Gaussian random variable in a Banach space

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Gaussian measure OurBigBook.com
A random variable X in a real separable Banach space B is Gaussian when ℓ(X) has a normal distribution for every continuous linear functional ℓ∈B∗. It is centered when all these expected values vanish. Its probability law is a Gaussian measure. Degenerate normal distributions are allowed.
Strict increase of a Gaussian norm distribution
Words: 77
Gaussian random variable in a Banach space OurBigBook.com
Suppose B is a nonzero separable Banach space, the Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian random variable in a Banach space is a dense subset of B, and every centered ball of positive radius has positive probability. Then t↦P(∥X∥B​≤t) is strictly increasing on (0,∞). For 0<a<b, choose h in that Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian random variable in a Banach space with ∥h∥B​=(a+b)/2 and 0<δ<(b−a)/2. The closed ball of radius δ centered at h lies in the annulus a<∥x∥B​<b and has positive probability by the symmetric Gaussian translation lower bound. The nonzero assumption is necessary: on B={0} the distribution function equals one everywhere.

Cameron-Martin theorem for a Gaussian measure

Gaussian measure OurBigBook.com
For μ=N(0,Σ) with injective covariance operator of a Gaussian measure, its translated law μh​=N(h,Σ) is an equivalent probability measure to μ if and only if h∈Eμ​, the Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian measure. For such h,
dμdμh​​(x)=exp(ℓh​(x)−21​∥h∥Eμ​2​),ℓh​(x)=∑j​λj​hj​xj​​.
(76)
The series has mean-square convergence and converges almost surely under μ, with normal distribution N(0,∥h∥Eμ​2​). Its exponential density has expected value one by the moment-generating function of a normal distribution. Finite-dimensional projections give the formula by ratios of multivariate normal densities; convergence of these likelihood ratios gives the infinite-dimensional result. The expression ⟨h,x⟩Eμ​​ is only formal when the sample is outside Eμ​. For h∈/Eμ​, translation gives mutually singular measures.
Symmetric Gaussian translation lower bound (P(X−h∈C)≥e−∥h∥H2​/2P(X∈C))

Cameron-Martin theorem for a Gaussian measure OurBigBook.com
For a centered Gaussian random variable in a Banach space, a Borel set C=−C, and h in its Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian random variable in a Banach space, the Cameron-Martin theorem for a Gaussian measure gives the translated density e−h(X)−∥h∥H2​/2. The joint law of (X,h(X)) is invariant under simultaneous negation. Averaging the two density formulas therefore replaces e−h(X) by coshh(X)≥1, proving the lower bound. No convexity of C is required.

Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian measure (Eμ​=RanΣ1/2)

Words: 181 Articles: 1
Gaussian measure OurBigBook.com
For a centered Gaussian measure on a real Hilbert space with injective covariance operator of a Gaussian measure Σ, its Cameron-Martin space is Eμ​=RanΣ1/2, with inner product ⟨h,g⟩Eμ​​=⟨Σ−1/2h,Σ−1/2g⟩. In an orthonormal basis satisfying Σej​=λj​ej​, it consists of exactly the vectors h for which ∑j​hj2​/λj​<∞. It is complete in this stronger norm even if its range is not closed in the ambient norm. Its importance is that it describes precisely the translations that preserve the null sets of the Gaussian measure, as in the Cameron-Martin theorem for a Gaussian measure. For generalized Gaussian white noise over L2, the corresponding Cameron-Martin space is L2 space itself.
Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian random variable in a Banach space (H=SG,Sg=E[Xg])
Words: 94
Cameron-Martin space of a Gaussian measure OurBigBook.com
Let G be the first Gaussian chaos of a centered Gaussian random variable in a Banach space. By Fernique's theorem, Sg=E[Xg] is a Bochner integral in B. The map S is injective, because Sg=0 implies E[gℓ(X)]=0 for every continuous linear functional ℓ, hence g=0. Its range becomes a Hilbert space under ⟨Sg,Sv⟩H​=E[gv]. The embedding in B is continuous by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Its reproducing property is ⟨h,Sℓ(X)⟩H​=ℓ(h). Thus this is the Reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the random variable, including degenerate laws. For h=Sg, the scalar coordinate h(X)=g has variance ∥h∥H2​; it is generally a measurable linear coordinate rather than a continuous functional on B.

The covariance operator K of a Gaussian measure on a real Hilbert space satisfies ⟨Kh,g⟩=Cov(⟨U,h⟩,⟨U,g⟩). A positive self-adjoint operator is the covariance of a Hilbert-space-valued Gaussian random variable exactly when it is trace class.

Bayesian inverse problem

Words: 215 Articles: 3
Gaussian measure OurBigBook.com
A Bayesian inverse problem combines a prior measure μ0​ on an unknown u with a likelihood for observed data y. When the likelihood is proportional to e−Φ(u;y), Bayes' formula gives
dμ0​dμy​(u)=Z(y)1​e−Φ(u;y).
(78)
Bayes formula for a dominated observation model
Words: 104
Bayesian inverse problem OurBigBook.com
Suppose an unknown has prior distribution Π and its conditional observation law Pu​ has jointly measurable Radon-Nikodym derivative L(u,m) relative to a fixed observation law P0​. If L>0 for Π(du)P0​(dm)-almost every pair, then
Z(m)=∫L(u,m)Π(du),dΠdΠm​(u)=Z(m)L(u,m)​
(79)
defines the posterior distribution for almost every observation. Indeed, ∫L(u,m)P0​(dm)=1 for almost every u, so Tonelli theorem gives ∫Z(m)P0​(dm)=1. Hence Z is finite almost everywhere, and positivity of L and Fubini's theorem give Z>0 almost everywhere. The data law is ZP0​, and integration of the proposed posterior against this data law recovers the joint law. This proves the conditional distribution property and also shows that the data law is an equivalent probability measure to P0​.
Well-posed Bayesian inverse problem in total variation
Words: 29
Bayesian inverse problem OurBigBook.com
A Bayesian inverse problem is well posed in total variation when a unique posterior exists for every datum and the map from data to posterior is continuous in total variation distance.
Well-posed Bayesian inverse problem in Hellinger distance
Words: 49
Bayesian inverse problem OurBigBook.com
A Bayesian inverse problem is well posed in Hellinger distance when every datum determines a unique posterior and the posterior depends continuously on the data in Hellinger distance. Since posterior measures are dominated by the prior and squared Hellinger distance is at most twice total variation distance, total-variation well-posedness implies Hellinger well-posedness.

Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process OurBigBook.com
For an adapted stationary process with the displayed bounds, the Itô formula and stationarity give ∫0t​(E[Zs​gs​]+λ)ds=0. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality makes each integrand nonnegative, so equality holds almost everywhere. Then E(gs​+λZs​)2≤0, proving g=−λZ for almost every time and outcome. Thus the process solves the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic differential equation and its initial value, rather than stationarity alone, determines its coupling with W.
Same-noise stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes (Zt​−Yt​=e−λt(Z0​−Y0​))
Words: 45
Stationary drift saturation OurBigBook.com
Two Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes with the same driving Brownian motion have the displayed difference. If Y0​ is standard normal and independent of future Brownian increments, replacing it by −Y0​ produces another stationary process with the same covariance and second moment, but a different pathwise coupling. Equal initial values are necessary for indistinguishability of stochastic processes.

Exponential Brownian time change to a stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (Yt​=e−λtBe2λt​)

Words: 72
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process OurBigBook.com
For λ>0, set Gt​=Fe2λt​ and Wt​=(2λ)−1/2∫1e2λt​u−1/2dBu​. This is a Brownian motion in the new filtration; its independent Gaussian increments have variance equal to elapsed time. The Itô product rule gives dY=2λ​dW−λYdt. Its initial value is B1​, independent of future W increments, and its covariance function is e−λ∣t−s∣. Consequently it is a stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. The quadratic variation of the unscaled time change is e2λt−1, not e2λt.

The linear stochastic differential equation has the explicit solution Yt​=e−λtY0​+σ∫0t​e−λ(t−s)dWs​. Its integrating factor is eλt. For λ>0, an independent initial normal variable of variance σ2/(2λ) makes its zero-mean Gaussian process stationary.

Squaring the stochastic kernel κ​τ[1−e−(t−u)/τ] and integrating proves this formula. The exponential moment of a Gaussian linear functional gives EBtn​=B0n​en2V(t)/2 and the displayed long-time growth exponent. Positive moment growth with zero mean strain reflects the breadth of the log-normal distribution; it does not imply positive growth of the mean logarithm.

Shifting and scaling to x=(σ−κnτ2)/κτ​ gives ψxx​+[1+κn2τ3−2γτ−x2]ψ=0. The quantum harmonic oscillator levels yield the displayed eigenvalues. Colored noise

Words: 31
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process OurBigBook.com
Colored noise has nonzero temporal correlation away from equal times. An Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise has exponential covariance and approaches white noise when its correlation time tends to zero at fixed integrated covariance.

Counting process (N(t))

Words: 218 Articles: 4
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A counting process is an integer-valued stochastic process that starts at zero and increases by recording the cumulative number of events up to each time.

Counting-process intensity (E(dN∣Ft−​)=λ(t)dt)

Words: 39
Counting process OurBigBook.com
A predictable intensity λ(t) is the derivative of an absolutely continuous compensator of a counting process: N(t)−∫0t​λ(u)du is a local martingale. It represents the conditional event rate given the immediately preceding history. In survival analysis the individual intensity is an at-risk indicator multiplied by its hazard function.

Counting-process intensity in survival analysis (E(dNi​∣Ht−​)=Yi​hi​dt)

Words: 32
Counting process OurBigBook.com
An observed event counting process has conditional increment E(dNi​(t)∣Ht−​)=Yi​(t)hi​(t)dt, where Yi​ is the at-risk process. The filtration records the past observed events, censoring, and covariates; the integral of Yi​hi​ is the compensator of a counting process.

Compensator of a counting process (Λ(t))

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Counting process OurBigBook.com
The compensator of a counting process N(t) is a predictable increasing process Λ(t) such that N(t)−Λ(t) is a local martingale. For an observed event process with at-risk process Y(t) and hazard function h(t), it is Λ(t)=∫0t​Y(u)h(u)du under independent censoring. It is cumulative intensity, rather than an event probability.

Counting-process martingale (M(t)=N(t)−∫0t​λ(u)du)

Words: 81
Compensator of a counting process OurBigBook.com
If a counting process N has predictable conditional intensity λ, subtracting its compensator of a counting process gives the associated martingale M. Conditional expected event increments and compensator increments agree, so their difference is conditionally centered. With the necessary integrability, M is a mean-zero martingale; for a simple no-ties process its predictable quadratic variation is ∫0t​λ(u)du. A predictable weighted martingale integral has mean zero and variance determined by the square of its weights. In survival analysis, λ=Yh produces the event-minus-expected representation used to derive the Nelson–Aalen estimator.
